Precept
PRE-sept
n. (a particular commandment or charge; rendering Hebrew piqqud, tsav, Greek entole)
From Latin praeceptum, from praecipere, to take beforehand, to instruct. A precept is a specific charge rather than a general principle — the particular, applied form of the law.

Biblical Definition

A precept is a particular charge laid on a particular people, and Psalm 119 makes it one of its eight words for the law of God. The psalmist states the manner as well as the fact: “Thou hast commanded us to keep thy precepts diligently” (Psalm 119:4) — not approximately, not in spirit only, but diligently. He then claims something more than obedience: “Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way” (Psalm 119:104). The order is worth marking, because it reverses the modern assumption. Understanding is not the precondition of obedience but its fruit; a man learns why God's way is right by walking in it, and the fruit of that understanding is not neutrality toward error but hatred of it. Isaiah gives the word its most quoted and most abused setting: “precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little” (Isaiah 28:10). And Jeremiah uses the word for a human father's charge with startling approval: the Rechabites had kept the precepts of Jonadab their father for generations, and God holds up their fidelity to a dead ancestor as a rebuke to Judah's infidelity to a living God (Jeremiah 35:18).

Webster 1828 Definition

A particular charge. Psalm 119 requires precepts kept diligently and says understanding comes through them rather than before them; Isaiah 28:10 is the famous line-upon-line text; Jeremiah commends the Rechabites for keeping their father's precepts.

PRECEPT, n. [L. praeceptum, from praecipio, to command; prae and capio.] In a general sense, any commandment or order intended as an authoritative rule of action.

2. In morality or religion, a commandment; a mandate; a rule directing moral conduct.

3. In law, a command or mandate in writing.

4. Doctrine; teaching; instruction; as the precepts of a master.

PRECEPTIVE, a. Containing precepts; giving rules or directions; didactic.

Key Scripture

Psalm 119:4 — "Thou hast commanded us to keep thy precepts diligently."

Psalm 119:104 — "Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way."

Isaiah 28:10 — "For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept; line upon line, line upon line; here a little, and there a little:"

Jeremiah 35:18 — "And Jeremiah said unto the house of the Rechabites, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Because ye have obeyed the commandment of Jonadab your father, and kept all his precepts, and done according unto all that he hath commanded you:"

Modern Corruption

Isaiah 28:10 is quoted as a positive method of Bible study — build doctrine line upon line — when in its own context it is the mocking speech of drunken scoffers imitating the prophet's tedious repetition, and God turns it back on them as judgment.

expand to see more

“Precept upon precept, line upon line” has furnished the title of Bible-study curricula and the motto of careful exposition, and the method it is used to commend is a good one. The verse itself is not commending it. Isaiah 28 opens with the drunkards of Ephraim; verse 9 asks contemptuously whom this prophet thinks he is teaching — children just weaned? — and verse 10 is the scoffers' mimicry of his preaching, a sing-song of baby-talk syllables in the Hebrew (tsav latsav, qav laqav). God's answer in verse 11 is that since they will not hear plain Hebrew, He will speak to them with stammering lips and another tongue — the Assyrian invader. The verse is a judgment on men who found God's word tediously elementary. That is a sharper word for the church than the study-method reading, and it is the one the text actually gives.

The deeper matter is what Psalm 119:104 says about how understanding is acquired. The modern instinct is to withhold obedience until the reason is clear: I will submit when I am persuaded. The psalmist reports the reverse order — through thy precepts I get understanding — and the Lord Jesus states it as a principle: if any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine (John 7:17). This is not anti-intellectualism; Psalm 119 is a long, deliberate meditation by a man who plainly thought hard. It is the claim that moral knowledge is not acquired at a distance, and that a man who will not keep the precepts he already understands will not be given more.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew piqqud (a precept, charge appointed, from paqad, to visit or appoint) and tsav (an injunction); Greek entole (a commandment) and entalma (a precept, used of the commandments of men).

expand to see more

Hebrew piqqud (H6490) — a precept, appointed charge; occurs 24 times, 21 of them in Psalm 119.

Hebrew paqad (H6485) — to visit, appoint, muster; the root, giving the precept its sense of something officially charged.

Hebrew tsav (H6673) — an injunction, precept; the word mimicked in Isaiah 28:10.

Greek entole (G1785) — a commandment, precept; the standard New Testament term.

Greek entalma (G1778) — a precept, injunction; used only of the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9; Colossians 2:22).

Usage

"“Keep thy precepts diligently” — the manner is commanded along with the matter."

"“Through thy precepts I get understanding” — understanding is the fruit of obedience, not its precondition."

"“Precept upon precept” — in context, the scoffers' mimicry of a prophet they found tedious."
